newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OSCE meets to study Belgrade reply over polls.
newsitem.headline: OSCE meets to study Belgrade reply over polls.

text.p: Yugoslavia on Friday accepted that opposition parties won a majority in nine municipalities in Belgrade in November 17 local elections but said it needed more detail to clarify results in others towns.

Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic wrote to the Vienna-based Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), acknowledging that the "coalition "Zajedno' won the majority in nine municipalities in Belgrade".
Milutinovic's letter was sent as a response to an OSCE report by former Spanish prime minister Felipe Gonzalez who led a mission to Serbia to investigate the disputed elections.

The OSCE sent Gonzalez after an invitation from Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic who has faced 46 days of protest over cancellation of the opposition victories in municipalities across the country and growing international criticism.
While the response may appear to be a sliver of a concession, the letter makes no mention of Milosevic's ruling Socialist Party handing over control of the capital.
The letter was addressed to Foreign Minister Niels Petersen of Denmark, which took over the chairmanship of the OSCE from Switzerland on January 1.
The Yugoslav foreign minister said authorities were still studying the election results in Serbia's second biggest city, Nis, which Gonzalez said had been won by the opposition.
He also called on Petersen to provide data on the OSCE findings on six other disputed municipalities to the Serbian authorities to help them clarify the election results.
One Vienna-based diplomatic source said the letter was "manipulative" and it appeared Belgrade was still playing for time.
The OSCE's decision-making permanent council was called into special session at 3 p.m. (1400 GMT) to discuss Gonzalez's report and Milutinovic's reply, OSCE officials said.
"We shall meet this afternoon and we shall want to support Mr Gonzalez's report fully," one OSCE delegation source said before the meeting began.
"The (Yugoslav) letter on a first reading does not look very clear but we shall want to show we are fully behind Gonzalez."
The permanent council may call on Belgrade to accept in full all Gonzalez's recommendations, a separate diplomatic source said.
In a first reaction to Milutinovic's letter, opposition Democratic Party leader Zoran Djindjic said the reply was unacceptable and was a rejection of the OSCE recommendations.
Gonzalez concluded in his OSCE report that the Zajedno coalition had fairly won the elections in 13 key provincial centres as well as in the nine municipalities in Belgrade.

It was not immediately clear what action the 54-member body can take against Yugoslavia if it ignores Gonzalez's recommendations. In 1992 the forum suspended Yugoslavia, now consisting of Serbia and Montenegro, accusing Belgrade of helping to stoke the war in neighbouring Bosnia.

But Milosevic is eager to be accepted back into the international diplomatic fold and being readmitted to the OSCE could herald rehabilitation into bodies such as the United Nations and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
